To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

E. coli O10, a hybrid pathotype of enteroaggregating and shiga toxigenic E. coli, was detected in feedlot cattle feces and the prevalence estimates were higher by PCR detection method compared to culture method.
cattle do not harbor and shed E. coli O 104:H4 pathogen, but they do harbor and excrete O 104 strains that are not pathogenic to humans.
E. coli O 104:H7 was detected in feedlot cattle feces, but the pathotype O104:H4 was not detected.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the detection, characterization and prevalence of O104 in feedlot cattle feces.
the prevalence, isolation and characterization of E. coli serogroup O104, which has been involved in human outbreaks of bloody diarrhea.
the prevalence and characterization of the O104:H7 hybrid pathotype in feedlot cattle.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the prevalence of the hybrid O104 pathotype in feedlot cattle was 0% (95% confidence interval [CI], 0 to 1.2%) by culture and 1.3% (95% CI, 0.5 to 2.2%) by PCR.
cattle do harbor and shed O104:H7 in the feces, and this serotype is associated with stx1 gene and has high genetic relatedness to the German outbreak and human diarrheagenics strains.
E. coli O106:H7 is the most predominant serogroup in cattle feces.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cattle do not harbor O104:H4 and O104:H21 strains that were associated with the German outbreak and human illness in 2011.
E. coli O101, O104, O105, O106, O107 and O108 serogroups were present in the feces of feedlots and the predominant serogroup was O107.
cattle do not harbor E. coli O157:H7 but they do harbor and excrete Shiga toxigenes of other serogroups.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cattle are a potential source of E. coli hybrid pathotype, which can contaminate the food chain and cause human infections.
cattle are an important reservoir of Shiga toxigentic O104 and the predominant serotypes are O104:H7.
cattle are a potential source of human exposure to Shiga toxigenics O104.
